To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the return of large carnivores to areas from which they have been absent for a long time raises specific questions, that the response by public authorities must respect the limits of the international and European nature and species protection law and that this law, in its current form, is not always sufficiently clear and flexible.

(1) international and European nature protection law provides a comprehensive framework for the management of carnivores returning to areas in which they have been extinct or nearly so, (2) this legal framework is based on the precautionary principle, (3) this framework is designed to ensure the survival and reproduction of the species, (4) the framework is not designed to protect the species from human beings, and (5) the framework is based on international and European law, and not national law

(i) the return of lynx, wolf and brown bear to Western Europe has been facilitated by the Bern Convention and Habitats Directive, which have created a legal obligation to conserve these species; (ii) this obligation has been further strengthened by the adoption of specific action plans; and (iii) the conservation status of the species is such that their reintroduction and/or transboundary management plans are not necessary.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the international and EU nature conservation law responds to the rewilding of Western Europe, and how this may be further developed in the light of the current comeback of large carnivores.
how to manage a comeback.
the legal framework for managing the carnivore comeback, which is increasingly a reality in Western Europe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current international and EU nature conservation regimes do not offer sufficient guarantees to effectively conserve large carnivore populations in Western Europe.
, although there is no single answer to the question how carnivore comebacks can be effectively managed, there is a clear legal obligation to do so.
the current legal framework for the conservation of large predators in Western Europe is not entirely adequate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the law is not yet fully equipped to deal with the return of large carnivores to Western Europe. This is not to say
the law is not a hindrance to the conservation of large carnivore populations in Europe, but rather an indispensable tool.
the law has a role to play in carnivore conservation in Western Europe, but that it is a limited one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while international and EU species protection law does not offer a comprehensive solution to the challenges posed by carnivore comebacks, it does provide a useful starting point.
international and EU species protection law is well equipped to address the return of large carnivores to Western Europe.
the international species protection regime has developed a set of legal tools that can effectively address the re-emergence of carnivores in Western Europe.
